entries.title: Trump Stumps for Alaska Republicans and Hands Out Two Pardons
entries.summary: The president handed out the pardons on stage to two mechanics who pleaded guilty to violating environmental laws.
entries.content:
President Donald Trump pardoned two mechanics on stage Tuesday in Alaska, clearing them of their guilty pleas to violating environmental laws.

Stumping for Republicans in Wasilla, Alaska, Trump announced the pardons of Zachary Czubak and Patrick Fleming, a pair of Alaskan mechanics who had pleaded guilty to violating the Clean Air Act. Trump described the pardons as “unconditional.”

“That means you’re as clean as a newborn baby’s ass,” Trump told the crowd, later adding that the pardons were “worth the eight hours in a plane.”

After signing and handing Fleming his pardon on stage, Trump told the pair to say something to the crowd. Czubak called for the reelection of the state’s congressional Republicans, who had lobbied Trump for the pardons. Fleming thanked the president for his freedom.

“This means the world to me,” Fleming said. “It really did destroy us.”

“We’re not criminals,” he added. “We’re not trying to hurt anybody. We want to help Alaskans.”

Trump also referenced Mackenzie Spurlock, another Alaskan mechanic who pleaded guilty to the same violation; the president pardoned Spurlock earlier this year.

Trump made the rare campaign stop in Alaska as the Republican Party makes its final push toward the midterms and politicians in the state hope for a boost in tough races.

Incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan has lagged behind Democratic challenger Mary Peltola in recent polls, while The Cook Political Report changed its outlook on Tuesday for the governor’s race in favor of Democratic candidate Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins.

Kreiss-Tomkins, a former state lawmaker, is the only Democrat in the four-person race for governor. With three Republican candidates, there’s potential for support to splinter between them and hand the race to Kreiss-Tomkins.
entries.author: Ben T.N. Mause

entries.title: Jon Ossoff Pledges to Serve a Full Term if He’s Reelected
entries.summary: The Democratic senator said he has “zero interest” in running for president as buzz about a potential 2028 campaign grows.
entries.content:
Sen. Jon Ossoff of Georgia pledged on Tuesday that he would serve a full Senate term if he’s reelected next month.

It’s a striking commitment given that Ossoff, who is running in a battleground state, has been floated as a 2028 presidential candidate and has proven himself to be a messaging leader for the Democratic Party.

His promise was made in a debate against Rep. Mike Collins, Ossoff’s Republican opponent in the Senate race, where he was asked almost immediately if he would stay in the Senate if reelected.

“Yes I will,” Ossoff, whose upcoming Senate term would run through the start of 2033 if reelected, replied. “I have zero interest in running for president. I'm not running for president. I'm running for reelection to the Senate.”

Ossoff has previously said he’s uninterested in seeking the presidency, but Tuesday’s pledge ruling it out was the most unequivocal statement he’s made in response to the question.

The candidates argued over affordability, health care, abortion and gun rights at the debate, which was their second time facing off.

Like last week, Ossoff used the stage to highlight Collins and his family and staffers’ ties to far-right views. The debate devolved as the two talked over each other.

Ossoff asked Collins if he would “stop the production of neo-Nazi propaganda from [his] home,” while Collins blamed Ossoff for death threats he’s received and sought to tie him to Hasan Piker, the far-left streamer whose comments about Israel have become campaign fodder.

Ossoff also hammered Collins over a pending ethics investigation into his office’s use of taxpayer funds, which Collins called a “nothing burger.”

While some Republicans in battleground states have distanced themselves from President Donald Trump by opposing certain policies, Collins has defended the Trump administration across both debates, with little exception.

Though Collins appeared to create a little daylight with the president when he was asked about federal intervention in elections, saying that “voting should always be a state's right,” he followed up by pitching the SAVE Act. The legislation, one of Trump’s top legislative priorities for months, would restrict voting access.

Ossoff has consistently led in the polls and enjoyed a huge fundraising advantage over Collins.

National Democrats, confident in Ossoff, appear to believe he’s on track for reelection: On Tuesday, the Chuck Schumer-aligned Senate Majority PAC said it was removing ad spending it had dedicated to Georgia.

Editor’s Note: This story has been updated with additional reporting.
entries.author: Hunter Riggall
